Fix Windows zombie Chrome/chromedriver processes (#78)

On Windows, ~170 Chrome/chromedriver processes were left behind after
`make test` because process cleanup used Unix-only tools (pgrep, SIGKILL)
that silently failed. Three root causes were fixed:

1. Process tree killing: killByPid() and killProcess() now use
   `taskkill /T /F /PID` on Windows to kill entire process trees
   instead of single-process Kill().

2. Graceful shutdown race: Skip the DELETE+sleep session teardown on
   Windows since it lets chromedriver exit before taskkill can kill its
   tree, orphaning Chrome children.

3. Error path cleanup: os.Exit(1) in CLI commands bypassed all defers,
   skipping browser cleanup. Added fatalExit() helper and KillAll()
   calls in printError() to ensure cleanup on error paths. Fixed the
   JS client's stop() and test helpers to use taskkill /T on Windows
   instead of SIGTERM (which maps to immediate TerminateProcess).

Queue client writes so a stalled reader can't freeze the session

ClientConn.Send did a synchronous websocket.WriteMessage under the connection
mutex, and routeBrowserToClient calls Send for every message forwarded from the
browser. Once a client stopped draining its socket and the kernel buffers
filled, that write blocked the pump — and with it the whole session. This is the
defect fixed for the pipe transport in #231, still live in the WebSocket one.

single writer goroutine, socket writes performed with no lock held, and a
watchdog that reports a write blocked for more than 5s.

Two differences from the pipe version, both because a socket can stall where a
pipe returns an error: each write gets a 60s deadline, and a failed write marks
the connection closed and drops it, so the queue cannot grow without bound
against a reader that never returns.

Session close probes the browser instead of stalling behind it

closeSession queued behind any in-flight recording command, so a
wedged command against a dead browser held teardown for the full
command timeout (#316). The issue's proposed fix — abort all pending
commands first — would have broken auto-finalize-on-close, which needs
the connection to deliver an active recording.

Probe instead: when the browser's state is unknown, one cheap getTree
bounded to two seconds decides the path. Alive → finalize over the
connection, then tear down, exactly as before. Dead → abort pending
commands first (the mutex frees immediately) and finalize offline:
package the trace from memory and embed the engine's live-muxed video
when it is readable and non-empty, with the manifest recording why the
video is cut short. When the routing goroutine triggers the close it
already watched the connection die, so it skips the probe entirely.

to 41ms, and the recording delivers instead of vanishing. The 60s was
mostly a second bug this surfaced: a client command racing session
deletion was dropped with no reply, leaving the client to wait out its
full send timeout — it now gets an immediate "browser session is
closed" error. The MCP surface gets the same probe before its
finalize.

Establish download behavior before serving client commands

setupDownloads ran in a bare goroutine, so a client whose first command
started a download could be served before the browser knew where to save
it, and the file landed outside the session's temp dir where
download.saveAs could not find it. Run it synchronously in
OnClientConnect, which completes before either transport reads client
messages, the same guarantee session.subscribe already relies on (#351).

The new test proves the ordering by holding the setDownloadBehavior
response from a fake remote endpoint, not by timing.

Test adapted from #354 by css521.

Gate commands behind event setup in the JS client

onWebSocket sent its install command fire-and-forget, so a socket opened
by the very next command could beat the install and the created event
was lost for good. The data-collector install behind onRequest and
onResponse had the same shape (#351).

Registration now goes through sendSetup, which parks a settle-only gate
that later sends wait on. Registration methods stay synchronous; the
next command completes the ordering. The dialog-unblock command bypasses
the gate, since an open dialog is what blocks the install ack, and a
command parked behind the gate fails fast if the connection closes
underneath it. The sync API blocks until the install is acknowledged and
raises if it was rejected, the only place a sync caller can see it.

The new tests drive the client against a stand-in engine that installs
slowly, so they assert ordering deterministically without a browser.

Gate commands behind event setup in the Python client

on_web_socket handed its install command to ensure_future and forgot
it, so a socket opened by the very next command could beat the install
and the created event was lost for good. The data-collector install
behind on_request and on_response had the same shape (#351).

Registration now goes through send_setup, which records a task that
send() waits for before dispatching. Registration methods stay
synchronous; the next command completes the ordering. The
dialog-unblock command bypasses the gate, a command parked behind the
gate fails fast when the connection closes, and the blocking sync API
waits for the install ack and raises if it was rejected.

Same stand-in-engine test approach as the JS client, plus a test that a
command held behind setup gets a connection error when the client
closes underneath it.

Delete the event-setup race workarounds

With setup acknowledged before the next command dispatches, the hedges
against the subscription race can go: the Python probe helper (which
had a residual straggler race of its own), the JS INSTALL_BARRIER_MS
wait, and the fixed post-registration waits in both sync websocket
suites. The downloads tutorial goes back to a single click; the poll
that remains waits for event arrival, not for the subscription.

The retry loop in prompt-blocked.test.js stays. That click's response
is blocked by the open alert by design, which is a different mechanism
from the subscription race (#351).

Retry a failed event-setup install on the next registration

A failed WebSocket monitor install left the page unrecoverable: the
install was keyed on the callback count, so later registrations never
re-sent it and their callbacks could never fire. Key it on the setup
state instead and reset that state on failure, the same recovery the
data-collector install already had.

Async registrations stay in place and start working once a retry
succeeds. The blocking sync APIs unregister the callback they added
before re-raising, so catching the error and retrying registers once
instead of delivering twice. The Python client now debug-logs a failed
install through the stdlib vibium logger, matching the JS client.

The stand-in engine counts install commands and reports the count
through a test back-channel eval, so the registering-twice tests assert
exactly one install was sent. A fail-once mode covers the retry path in
all four suites.

Bound the download setup command to 10 seconds

Establishing download behavior synchronously in OnClientConnect meant a
browser that wedged on setDownloadBehavior held every client command for
the full 60 second default. The failure outcome is the same at any
timeout, downloads land in the browser's default directory, so the only
thing the timeout controls is how long connect appears hung first. The
error log now states that consequence.

Fix two capture races that let stale events satisfy a wait

Both failures came from an event emitted before the wait started being
delivered after it started.

remove_all_listeners network tests: the callback is registered after
go(), so a late response from the navigation itself can land in the
window between subscribing and removing, and "any response" counted it.
Scoped the four tests -- Python and JS, request and response -- to
/api/data, the URL doFetch() actually requests, matching what the
neighbouring assertions in the same files already do. Verified the
scoped tests still fail when remove_all_listeners is stubbed out, so
the narrowing did not neuter them.

Capture.navigation: actionStarted only rejects events seen before the
action begins. page.go() returns when navigation completes but its
event is delivered asynchronously, so a stale one arrives after the
flag flips, and value -> true accepted it -- returning the previous URL.
capture().request/response were immune because their URL pattern
filtered it. navigation now waits for a move away from the page's
current URL.

That trade-off is deliberate: a navigation to the URL the page is
already on is no longer captured. Completing on a stale event and
returning the wrong URL is the worse failure.
